Seamy means sordid, morally unpleasant, and corrupt — the kind of dark, dirty, or shameful side of something that most people prefer not to look at or talk about openly.

Think of it as describing the ugly, hidden underbelly of something that otherwise appears respectable or normal on the surface. When you call something "seamy," you are pointing to the parts of it that involve dishonesty, vice, moral corruption, or social disgrace.

The word "seamy" can describe:

Situations and events
A seamy affair, a seamy deal, seamy details — these are situations involving scandal, corruption, or moral wrongdoing. For example, a business deal that involves bribery, manipulation, and secret agreements behind closed doors would be called seamy.

Places
A seamy neighborhood or a seamy bar is a place associated with crime, vice, prostitution, drug use, or general moral degradation. It is a place that feels threatening, corrupt, and socially unacceptable.

A side or aspect of something
The most classic use of "seamy" is in the phrase "the seamy side" — meaning the hidden, corrupt, or ugly dimension of something. You might hear about "the seamy side of Hollywood," referring to the exploitation, abuse, and corruption that exists beneath all the glamour. Or "the seamy side of politics" — the backroom deals, blackmail, and dishonesty that the public rarely sees.

People and behavior
If someone has a seamy past or seamy reputation, it means their history involves disreputable or morally shameful actions — things like crime, scandal, or vice.

"Seamy" is a strongly negative word. It does not just mean slightly unpleasant or mildly uncomfortable. It carries a sense of moral degradation and disgust — the feeling you get when you see something that violates basic standards of decency and honesty.

It also carries a sense of hiddenness — seamy things are usually things that are concealed, that happen in the shadows, and that people are ashamed to expose to the light. When something seamy is revealed, it feels like turning over a rock and seeing what was rotting underneath.

The word has a somewhat literary or journalistic tone. You are more likely to encounter it in a novel, a documentary, an investigative article, or formal speech than in everyday casual conversation. That said, it is not so rare that people would find it strange — it is a well-understood word.

• "The journalist spent years investigating the seamy world of human trafficking."
    → Here, "seamy" tells us this world is morally corrupt, hidden, and deeply unpleasant.
  • "Behind its glamorous exterior, the film industry has a seamy side that rarely makes headlines."
    → The contrast between "glamorous exterior" and "seamy side" is exactly what the word is built for.
  • "He had lived a seamy life in his younger years — fraud, petty crime, and associations with dangerous people."
    → Here it describes a person's past as full of dishonest and morally degrading activity.
  • "The novel pulls no punches in depicting the seamy underbelly of Victorian London."
    → "Seamy underbelly" is a very common and powerful phrase, referring to the corrupt, criminal, and poverty-stricken parts of a society that the wealthy and powerful prefer to ignore.

• "the seamy side" — by far the most common usage; refers to the dark, corrupt aspect of something
  • "the seamy underbelly" — an intensified version; "underbelly" reinforces the idea of a soft, hidden, vulnerable, and ugly underside
  • "seamy details" — the unpleasant, morally troubling specifics of a scandal or crime
How It Differs from Similar Words

Seamy vs. sleazy
Both words describe moral corruption and unpleasantness. "Sleazy" is more casual and colloquial — you'd use it in everyday speech. "Seamy" is slightly more formal and literary. "Sleazy" often focuses on sexual impropriety or cheapness in a more direct way. "Seamy" is broader — it covers all kinds of moral degradation, corruption, and vice, not just sexual sleaziness.

Seamy vs. sordid
These are very close in meaning, and you can often use them interchangeably. "Sordid" emphasizes filth, baseness, and the mercenary or self-interested nature of something — people doing immoral things for money or selfish gain. "Seamy" is slightly broader and focuses more on the hidden, disreputable, shadowy nature of something. A sordid affair is one driven by base motives; a seamy affair is one that is shameful and would not survive being brought into the open.

Seamy vs. shady
"Shady" is casual and lighter — it hints at suspicion and dishonesty without the same degree of moral condemnation. "Seamy" is stronger and more serious, implying actual moral corruption rather than just suspicion of it.

"Seamy" sits firmly in the zone of strong moral condemnation. It is not a mild word. If you describe something as seamy, you are saying it involves genuine corruption, vice, or shame — not just mild awkwardness or minor impropriety.

If you want one sentence to anchor the word in your memory: seamy describes the dark, hidden, morally corrupt side of something — the part that decent people prefer not to see, that thrives in shadows, and that reveals the worst of human behavior when exposed.
